Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

In the matrix equation \(Px = q\), which of the following is a necessary condition for the existence of at least one solution for the unknown vector \(x\):
options: Augmented matrix \([P \quad q]\) must have the same rank as matrix \(P\)
Vector \(q\) must have only non-zero elements
questions.explanation:
According to the Rouché-Capelli theorem, a system of linear equations represented in matrix form as \(PX = Q\) is consistent if and only if the rank of the coefficient matrix \(P\) is identical to the rank of its augmented matrix \([P \mid Q]\). \[\rho(P) = \rho([P \mid Q])\]
  1. Unique Solution: If \(\rho(P) = \rho([P \mid Q]) = n\), the linear system has exactly one unique solution.
  2. Infinitely Many Solutions: If \(\rho(P) = \rho([P \mid Q]) < n\), the system has an infinite number of solutions.
\[\boxed{\text{(A) Augmented matrix $[P \quad q]$ must have the same rank as matrix $P$}}\]

Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

If \[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\], the top row of \(R^{-1}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Given the \(3 \times 3\) square matrix \(R\): \[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[R^{-1} = \frac{\text{adj}(R)}{|R|}\] \[|R| = 1 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} - 0 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + (-1) \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix}\] \[|R| = 1 \left[(1)(2) - (-1)(3)\right] - 0 - 1 \left[(2)(3) - (1)(2)\right]\] \[|R| = 1(2 + 3) - 1(6 - 2) = 5 - 4 = 1\] \[\text{adj}(R) = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11} & C_{21} & C_{31} \\ \times & \times & \times \\ \times & \times & \times \end{bmatrix}\]
  • \[C_{11} = (-1)^{1+1} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \cdot \left[(1)(2) - (-1)(3)\right] = 2 + 3 = 5\]
  • \[C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = -1 \cdot \left[(0)(2) - (-1)(3)\right] = -(0 + 3) = -3\]
  • \[C_{31} = (-1)^{3+1} \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \cdot \left[(0)(-1) - (-1)(1)\right] = 0 + 1 = 1\]
\[\text{adj}(R) = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1 \\ \times & \times & \times \\ \times & \times & \times \end{bmatrix}\] \[R^{-1} = \frac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1 \\ \times & \times & \times \\ \times & \times & \times \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1 \\ \times & \times & \times \\ \times & \times & \times \end{bmatrix}\] Therefore, the top row of \(R^{-1}\) is \[\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]. \[\boxed{\text{(B) $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$}}\]

questions.question: If \(S = \int_{1}^{\infty} x^{-3} \, dx\) then \(S\) has the value
questions.explanation:
The given integral to evaluate is: \[S = \int_{1}^{\infty} x^{-3} \, dx\] Using the standard power rule for integration, \(\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\) (for \(n \neq -1\)), we get: \[S = \left[ \frac{x^{-3+1}}{-3+1} \right]_{1}^{\infty}\] Simplifying the expression: \[S = \left[ \frac{x^{-2}}{-2} \right]_{1}^{\infty}\] \[S = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{1}{x^2} \right]_{1}^{\infty}\] Applying the upper and lower limits: \[S = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{1}{\infty^2} - \frac{1}{1^2} \right]\] Since \(\frac{1}{\infty} = 0\): \[S = -\frac{1}{2} [0 - 1]\] \[S = \frac{1}{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }\;\frac{1}{2}}\]
Key points
  • The improper integral of the form \(\int_{1}^{\infty} x^{-p} \, dx\) converges if and only if \(p > 1\).
  • Power rule of integration: \(\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C\).

questions.question: For the function \(f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\), the maximum occurs when \(x\) is equal to
questions.explanation:
The given function is: \[f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\] To find the points of local maxima or minima, we use the first derivative test by setting \(f'(x) = 0\). Using the product rule for differentiation \(\frac{d}{dx}[uv] = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}\): \[f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) \cdot e^{-x} + x^2 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(e^{-x})\] \[f'(x) = 2x e^{-x} + x^2 (-e^{-x})\] \[f'(x) = (2x - x^2) e^{-x}\] To find the stationary points, set \(f'(x) = 0\): \[(2x - x^2) e^{-x} = 0\] Since \(e^{-x} \neq 0\) for any real value of \(x\): \[2x - x^2 = 0\] \[x(2 - x) = 0\] This gives the stationary points: \[x = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad x = 2\] To determine where the maximum occurs, we use the second derivative test. Let's find \(f''(x)\): \[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \left[ (2x - x^2) e^{-x} \right]\] Applying the product rule again: \[f''(x) = (2 - 2x) e^{-x} + (2x - x^2) (-e^{-x})\] \[f''(x) = (2 - 2x - 2x + x^2) e^{-x}\] \[f''(x) = (x^2 - 4x + 2) e^{-x}\] Now, test the second derivative at the stationary points: **Case 1: At \(x = 0\)** \[f''(0) = (0^2 - 4(0) + 2) e^{0} = 2(1) = 2\] Since \(f''(0) > 0\), the function has a local **minimum** at \(x = 0\). **Case 2: At \(x = 2\)** \[f''(2) = (2^2 - 4(2) + 2) e^{-2} = (4 - 8 + 2) e^{-2} = -2 e^{-2}\] Since \(f''(2) < 0\), the function has a local **maximum** at \(x = 2\). Thus, the maximum occurs when \(x\) is equal to \(2\). \[\boxed{\text{(a)}\;2}\]
Key points
  • Stationary points are determined by setting the first derivative equal to zero: \(f'(x) = 0\).
  • **Second Derivative Test:**
    • If \(f''(c) < 0\), then \(f(x)\) has a local maximum at \(x = c\).
    • If \(f''(c) > 0\), then \(f(x)\) has a local minimum at \(x = c\).

questions.question: The solution of the first order differential equation \(\dot{x}(t)=-3x(t),\ x(0)=x_0\) is:
questions.explanation:
The given first-order differential equation is \[\dot{x}(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = -3x(t),\ \ \text{with the initial condition}\ \ x(0) = x_0\] We are required to determine \(x(t)\).
Method 1
The equation is separable. Hence, Integrating both sides, \[\int \frac{dx}{x} = -3\int dt.\] \[\ln|x| = -3t + C\] \[x = e^{-3t}\times e^C\] Applying the initial condition \(x(0) = x_0 = e^C\), Hence, \[x(t) =x _0\,e^{-3t}.\]
Method 2
Recognize the standard exponential response \[\frac{dx}{dt} = ax\] The solution is \[x(t) = x(0)e^{at},\ \text{where}\ a = -3\] Therefore, \[x(t) = x_0\,e^{-3t}\] This is the standard natural response of a stable first-order system.
\[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ x(t) = x_0\,e^{-3t}}\]
Key points
  • Such equations commonly model RC circuits, RL circuits, population decay, and thermal cooling.

questions.question: For the equation \(\ddot{x}(t)+3\dot{x}(t)+2x(t)=5,\) the solution \(x(t)\) approaches the following values at \(t\rightarrow \infty\)
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is \[\ddot{x}(t) + 3\dot{x}(t) + 2x(t) = 5\] We are required to determine \(\lim_{t\to\infty} x(t).\)
Method 1
The complete solution is the sum of the homogeneous solution and the particular solution: \[x(t) = x_h(t) + x_p(t)\] For the homogeneous part, \[\ddot{x} + 3\dot{x} + 2x = 0\] Assuming \(x=e^{mt}\), \[m^2 + 3m + 2 = 0\] \[(m+1)(m+2) = 0\] Hence, \[m_1 = -1,\qquad m_2 = -2\] Therefore, \[x_h(t) = C_1e^{-t} + C_2e^{-2t}\] Since the forcing function is a constant, assume a constant particular solution \(x_p = A.\) Substituting into the differential equation, \[0 + 0 + 2A = 5 \Rightarrow\ A=\frac{5}{2}\] Thus, \[x(t) = C_1e^{-t} + C_2e^{-2t} + \frac{5}{2}\] As \(t\to\infty\), \[e^{-t}\to 0, \qquad e^{-2t}\to 0.\] Therefore, \[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \frac{5}{2}\]
Method 2
Apply the Final Value Theorem. Taking Laplace transforms with arbitrary initial conditions, \[(s^2+3s+2)X(s)-\text{(initial-condition terms)} = \frac{5}{s}\] The terms arising from initial conditions contain factors of \(s\) and vanish when the final value theorem is applied. Thus, for steady-state analysis, \[X(s) = \frac{5}{s(s^2+3s+2)}\] Using \[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \lim_{s\to 0}sX(s),\] we obtain \[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \lim_{s\to 0} = \frac{5}{2}.\]
Method 3
At steady state, \[\dot{x}(t) = 0, \qquad \ddot{x}(t) = 0\] Substituting these conditions \[\ddot{x} + 3\dot{x} + 2x = 5\] \[2x_{\text{ss}} = 5\] \[x_{\text{ss}} = \frac{5}{2}\] Since the characteristic roots are \(-1,\,-2,\) the system is stable and all transient terms decay to zero. Hence, \[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = x_{\text{ss}} = \frac{5}{2}\]
Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\ \frac{5}{2}}\]
Key points
  • For stable systems, the transient terms vanish as \(t\to\infty\).
  • A constant forcing function generally produces a constant steady-state response.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the limit is zero simply because the homogeneous solution decays.
  • The Final Value Theorem can be used only when all poles of \(sX(s)\) lie in the left-half plane.

questions.question: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two random events, then which of the following is true?
options: Independence of \(P\) and \(Q\) implies that Probability \((P \cap Q)=0\)
If \(P\) and \(Q\) are mutually exclusive then they must be independent
questions.explanation: We check each statement using probability properties. For option A: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are independent, \[P(P\cap Q)=P(P)\,P(Q)\] This is not necessarily zero. Hence, option A is false. For option B: Using the addition theorem, \[P(P\cup Q)=P(P)+P(Q)-P(P\cap Q)\] Therefore, \[P(P\cap Q)=P(P)+P(Q)-P(P\cup Q)\] Since \[P(P\cup Q)\leq 1\] option B is not always true. Hence, option B is false. For option C: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are mutually exclusive, \[P(P\cap Q)=0\] But for independence, \[P(P\cap Q)=P(P)\,P(Q)\] These are equal only if one event has zero probability. Hence, mutually exclusive events are not necessarily independent. So, option C is false. For option D: Since \[P\cap Q \subseteq P\] we must have \[P(P\cap Q)\leq P(P)\] Hence, option D is true. \[\boxed{\text{(d) }P(P\cap Q)\leq P(P)}\]

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times in succession. If the first toss produces a head, then the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses is
questions.explanation: Let the event that the first toss is a head be \[F\] Given that the first toss is already a head, to get exactly two heads in three tosses, we need exactly one more head in the remaining two tosses. Possible outcomes for the last two tosses are: \[HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\] Favourable outcomes: \[HT,\ TH\] Hence, \[P(\text{exactly two heads}\mid F)=\frac{2}{4}\] \[=\frac{1}{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }\frac{1}{2}}\]

A coil of inductance \(10\text{H}\) resistance \(40\ \Omega\) is connected as shown in figure. After the switch S has been in connected with point 1 for a very long time, it is moved to point 2 at \(t = 0\).

If, at \(t = 0+\), the voltage across the coil is \(120\text{V}\), the value of resistance R is:
questions.explanation: For \(t<0\), the switch is connected to position 1 for a long time. Hence, the circuit is in steady state and the inductor behaves as a short circuit. Therefore, the current through the inductor just before switching is \[i_L(0^-) = \frac{120}{20+40} = 2~\text{A}\] Since the current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, \[i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-) = 2~\text{A}\] At \(t=0^+\), the source is disconnected and the inductor behaves as a constant current source of value \(i_L(0^+)=2~\text{A}\) The voltage across the coil is equal to the voltage drop across the external resistors \(R\) and \(20\Omega\), \[V_L = i_L(0^+)(R+20)\] Given that \[V_L = 120~\text{V}\] \[120 = 2(R+20)\] \[R+20 = 60=40~\Omega\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }40~\Omega}\]

For the value of R obtained in Q2.05.2, the time taken for \(95\%\) of the stored energy dissipated is close to
questions.explanation: From Q.2.05.2, For \(t>0\), the inductor discharges through the resistive network. The equivalent resistance seen by the inductor is \[R_{\text{eq}} = 40+40+20 = 100~\Omega\] The time constant is \[\tau = \frac{L}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{10}{100} = 0.1~\text{s}\] For a source-free RL circuit, \[i_L(t) = i_L(0^+)e^{-t/\tau}\] Substituting \[i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)=2~\text{A}\] \[i_L(t) = 2e^{-10t}\] The initial energy stored in the inductor is \[W_0 = \frac{1}{2}Li_L^2(0^-)= \frac{1}{2}\times10\times(2)^2\] \[W_0 = 20~\text{J}\] If \(95\%\) of the energy is dissipated, then only \(5\%\) remains: \[W = 0.05W_0= 0.05\times20\] \[W = 1~\text{J}\] Using \[W = \frac{1}{2}Li_L^2\] (where \(i_L\) is the current in the inductor after \(95\%\) dissipation of energy) \[\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\times10\times i_L^2 = 1 \ \Rightarrow \ i_L^2 = \frac{1}{5}\] \[i_L = \frac{1}{\sqrt5} = 0.4472~\text{A}\] Substituting into the current expression, \[2e^{-10t} = 0.4472\] \[e^{-10t} = 0.2236 \ \Rightarrow \ -10t = \ln(0.2236)\] \[t = 0.15~\text{s}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }0.15~\text{s}}\]

questions.question: The RL circuit of Figure is fed from a constant magnitude, variable frequency sinusoidal voltage source \(V_{IN}\). At 100 Hz, the R and L elements each have a voltage drop \(U_{RMS}\). If the frequency of the source is changed to 50 Hz, the new voltage drop across R is :
questions.explanation: Analysis of the series \(RL\) circuit at two different operating frequencies: Case 1: At frequency \(f_{1} = 100\,\text{Hz}\) The current \(I_{1}\) flowing through the circuit is given by: \[I_{1} = \frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_{L1}^2}}\] The voltage drop across each component is equal to \(V_{RMS}\), such that: \[V_{RMS} = I_{1} R = I_{1} |X_{L1}|\] Since the current \(I_{1}\) is identical throughout the series loop, we have: \[R = |X_{L1}|\] The voltage drop across the resistor \(R\) is in phase with the current \(I_{1}\), while the voltage drop across the inductor \(L\) leads the current \(I_{1}\) by \(90^\circ\) (the two voltages are in quadrature). Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) in phasor form: \[V_{in}^2 = V_{RMS}^2 + V_{RMS}^2 = 2 V_{RMS}^2\] \[V_{in} = \sqrt{2} V_{RMS}\] Case 2: At frequency \(f_{2} = 50\,\text{Hz}\) When the frequency is halved from \(100\,\text{Hz}\) to \(50\,\text{Hz}\), the new inductive reactance \(X_{L2}\) becomes: \[X_{L2} = \frac{X_{L1}}{2} = 0.5 X_{L1}\] Since \(R = |X_{L1}|\), we can express the resistance in terms of the new reactance: \[R = 2 X_{L2}\] The circuit current \(I_{2}\) at \(50\,\text{Hz}\) is: \[I_{2} = \frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_{L2}^2}}\] Performing voltage division to find the magnitude of the voltage across the resistor \(V_{R}\): \[V_{R} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_{L2}^2}} V_{in}\] Substituting \(R = |X_{L1}|\) and \(X_{L2} = 0.5 |X_{L1}|\): \[V_{R} = \frac{|X_{L1}|}{\sqrt{|X_{L1}|^2 + (0.5 |X_{L1}|)^2}} V_{in}\] \[V_{R} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 0.25}} V_{in} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.25}} V_{in} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} V_{in}\] Substituting \(V_{in} = \sqrt{2} V_{RMS}\) into the equation: \[V_{R} = \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{5}} V_{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{8}{5}} V_{RMS}\] \[\boxed{(c)\sqrt{\frac{8}{5}}V_{RMS}}\]

questions.question: Two networks are connected in cascade as shown in Figure. With the usual notations the equivalent \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) constants are obtained. Given that \(C = 0.025\angle 45^{\circ}\), the value of \(Z_2\) is:
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Based on the provided circuit analysis of cascaded two-port networks, we determine the equivalent ABCD parameters by multiplying the individual transmission matrices. 1. Series Impedance Element (\(Z_1\)) For a series impedance \(Z_1\), the transmission (ABCD) matrix is given by: \[\begin{bmatrix} A_1 & B_1 \\ C_1 & D_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & Z_1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] 2. Shunt Admittance Element (\(Z_2\)) For a shunt impedance \(Z_2\), the transmission (ABCD) matrix is given by: \[\begin{bmatrix} A_2 & B_2 \\ C_2 & D_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{Z_2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] 3. Cascaded Network Parameters The equivalent ABCD parameters of the cascaded connection are found by taking the product of the individual matrices: \[\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix}_{eq} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & Z_1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{Z_2} & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + \frac{Z_1}{Z_2} & Z_1 \\ \frac{1}{Z_2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] From the equivalent matrix, the parameter \(C\) is defined as: \[C = \frac{1}{Z_2}\] Given that: \[C = 0.025 \angle 45^{\circ}\,\text{S}\] Therefore, the shunt impedance \(Z_2\) is calculated as: \[Z_2 = \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{0.025 \angle 45^{\circ}} = 40 \angle -45^{\circ}\,\Omega\]
Method 2
Alternatively, we can calculate \(Z_2\) by directly computing the coefficient \(C\) without using the concept of cascade connection. The transmission parameters (\(ABCD\) parameters) equations are defined as: \[V_1 = A V_2 - B I_2\] \[I_1 = C V_2 - D I_2\] The coefficient \(C\) is given by: \[C = \left. \frac{I_1}{V_2} \right|_{I_2 = 0} \quad \text{(port 2 must be open)}\] From the circuit diagram, when port 2 is open (\(I_2 = 0\)), the current \(I_1\) flows entirely through the impedance \(Z_2\). Therefore: \[V_2 = I_1 Z_2\] Thus, the parameter \(C\) is: \[C = \frac{I_1}{V_2} = \frac{1}{Z_2}\] Given that: \[C = 0.025 \angle 45^\circ\] We can solve for \(Z_2\): \[Z_2 = \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{0.025 \angle 45^\circ} = 40 \angle -45^\circ\,\Omega\]
\[\boxed{(b)40 \angle -45^{\circ}\,\Omega}\]

questions.question: Assume that the \(N\)-channel \(MOSFET\) shown in figure is ideal, and that its threshold voltage is \(1\,\text{V}\). The voltage \(V_{ab}\) between nodes '\(a\)' and '\(b\)' is
questions.explanation:
From the given circuit, the gate voltage (\(V_G\)) is connected to a \(2\,\text{V}\) source, and the source terminal (\(V_S\)) is connected to ground (\(0\,\text{V}\)). The gate-to-source voltage is calculated as: \[V_{GS} = V_G - V_S = 2\,\text{V} - 0\,\text{V} = 2\,\text{V}\] The threshold voltage of the \(N\)-channel MOSFET is given as \(V_T = 1\,\text{V}\). Since \(V_{GS} > V_T\) (\(2\,\text{V} > 1\,\text{V}\)), the MOSFET is turned ON. Because the MOSFET is specified as "ideal" and no conduction parameters (such as \(\mu_n C_{ox}\) or \(W/L\)) are provided, it is modeled as an ideal switch. When turned ON, an ideal MOSFET acts as a short circuit between the drain and source terminals. \[V_D = V_S = 0\,\text{V}\] Node '\(a\)' is connected to the drain terminal through a \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor, and it is connected to ground (node '\(b\)') through a \(2\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor. Since the drain terminal is effectively at ground potential (\(V_D = 0\,\text{V}\)) and node '\(b\)' is also at ground (\(0\,\text{V}\)), there is no potential difference to drive current through this rightmost branch. Therefore, the voltage at node '\(a\)' is \(0\,\text{V}\). \[V_{ab} = V_a - V_b = 0\,\text{V} - 0\,\text{V} = 0\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }\text{0V}}\]
Key points
  • In the absence of specific transconductance parameters, an "ideal" MOSFET operates as a perfect switch.
  • When \(V_{GS} > V_T\), the ideal MOSFET is in the ON state and behaves as a short circuit (\(V_{DS} = 0\,\text{V}\)).
  • When the drain is shorted to ground, any parallel resistive branches connected to the drain will have \(0\,\text{V}\) across them, resulting in zero current and zero voltage drop across those components.

questions.question: The charge distribution in a metal-dielectric-semiconductor specimen is shown in Figure. The negative charge density decreases linearly in the semiconductor as shown. The electric field distribution is as shown in
questions.explanation: In a metal, all free charges reside on the surface. Hence, the electric field inside the metal is, E=0. The dielectric contains no free charge. Therefore, the electric field remains constant throughout the dielectric region. In the semiconductor, negative space charge is distributed throughout the depletion region. Consider a Gaussian surface starting at the oxide-semiconductor interface and extending a distance \(x\) into the semiconductor. As the Gaussian surface moves deeper into the semiconductor, it encloses more negative charge. From Gauss's law, \[\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon},\] the enclosed negative charge reduces the net electric flux. Therefore, the electric field decreases with increasing distance inside the semiconductor. Since the charge density decreases linearly, the slope of the electric field also decreases linearly, and the electric field finally becomes zero at the edge of the depletion region. Hence, the electric field distribution is \[\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Region} & \textbf{Electric Field} \\ \hline \text{Metal} & E=0 \\ \hline \text{Dielectric} & \text{Constant} \\ \hline \text{Semiconductor} & \text{Decreases linearly to zero} \\ \hline \end{array}\] Therefore, the correct electric field variation is shown in \[\boxed{\textbf{A}}\]

questions.question: Consider the inverting amplifier, using an ideal operational amplifier shown in Figure. The designer wishes to realize the input resistance seen by the small signal source to be as large as possible, while keeping the voltage gain between \(-10\) and \(-25\), the upper limit on \(R_F\) is \(1\text{ M}\Omega\). The value of \(R_1\) should be
questions.explanation:
The voltage gain of the inverting amplifier is: \[A_v = \frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{R_F}{R_1}\] The input resistance seen by the source is: \[R_{\text{in}} = R_1\] To maximize \(R_{\text{in}}\), \(R_1\) must be made as large as possible without violating the gain specification \(-25 \le A_v \le -10\). With \(R_F \le 1\,\text{M}\Omega = 1000\,\text{k}\Omega\):
  • For a gain magnitude of \(25\): \[R_1 = \frac{R_F}{25} \le \frac{1000\,\text{k}\Omega}{25} = 40\,\text{k}\Omega\]
  • For a gain magnitude of \(10\): \[R_1 = \frac{R_F}{10} \le \frac{1000\,\text{k}\Omega}{10} = 100\,\text{k}\Omega\]
To ensure that the full required gain magnitude range up to \(25\) can be achieved with \(R_F \le 1\,\text{M}\Omega\), \(R_1\) cannot exceed \(40\,\text{k}\Omega\). If \(R_1 = 100\,\text{k}\Omega\), the maximum achievable magnitude of gain is \(\frac{1\,\text{M}\Omega}{100\,\text{k}\Omega} = 10\), failing to reach a gain of \(-25\). Therefore, the maximum permissible value of \(R_1\) is \(40\,\text{k}\Omega\). \[\boxed{(D) \ \ 40 \text{ k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • Inverting Amplifier Input Resistance: The input impedance seen by \(V_{\text{in}}\) is \(R_1\) due to the virtual ground at the inverting node.
  • Upper Limit Constraint: Maximize \(R_1\) while ensuring \(R_F = R_1 \times |A_v|_{\max} \le R_{F,\max}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not choose \(R_1 = 100\,\text{k}\Omega\) by evaluating only the minimum gain condition, as it makes higher gains impossible under the \(R_F \le 1\,\text{M}\Omega\) constraint.

questions.question: Select the circuit which will produce the given output \(Q\) for the input signals \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) given in the figure.
questions.explanation:
Given: Waveforms for inputs \(X_1\), \(X_2\), and output \(Q\). 1. Functional Analysis from Waveforms:
By tracking the signal levels step-by-step from the given timing diagram, we observe the following behavior for output \(Q\):
  • When \((X_1, X_2) = (1, 0) \Rightarrow Q\) becomes \(1\) (Set operation).
  • When \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 0) \Rightarrow Q\) maintains its value at \(1\) (Hold operation).
  • When \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 1) \Rightarrow Q\) becomes \(0\) (Reset operation).
  • When \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 0) \Rightarrow Q\) maintains its value at \(0\) (Hold operation).
Summarizing this operational sequence gives us the function table of an active-HIGH cross-coupled NOR latch where \(X_1\) behaves as the Set (\(S\)) input and \(X_2\) behaves as the Reset (\(R\)) input: \[Q^+ = \overline{X_2 + \bar{Q}}, \quad \bar{Q}^+ = \overline{X_1 + Q}\] 2. Evaluation of Latch Options:
Let us evaluate each option by directly testing the node explicitly labeled \(Q\) against the established mathematical latch equations:
  • Option (A): This circuit shows a standard cross-coupled NOR latch configuration. Let the output of the bottom NOR gate be named \(W\). The expressions for the two gates are: \[Q = \overline{X_1 + W} \quad \text{and} \quad W = \overline{X_2 + Q}\] Let us apply the first input condition from the waveform: \((X_1, X_2) = (1, 0)\). Substituting \(X_1 = 1\) gives \(Q = \overline{1 + W} = 0\). This directly contradicts the waveform sequence, which explicitly shows that \(Q\) must go HIGH (\(1\)) when \((X_1, X_2) = (1, 0)\). Thus, Option (A) is incorrect.
  • Option (B): This circuit uses OR gates with cross-coupling instead of NOR gates. The labeled output node satisfies \(Q = X_1 + W\). If \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 0)\), the circuit simplifies to \(Q = 0 + W = W\), and \(W = 0 + Q = Q\). This creates an un-complemented feedback loop that cannot hold a distinct stable \((Q, \bar{Q})\) pair. Thus, Option (B) is incorrect.
  • Option (C): This configuration features an AND gate cross-coupled with a NAND gate. The node \(Q\) is driven by the AND gate: \(Q = X_1 \cdot W\). If \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 1)\), then \(X_1 = 0\) forces \(Q = 0 \cdot W = 0\), which matches the waveform reset condition. However, when inputs transition to the hold state \((X_1, X_2) = (0, 0)\), \(X_1 = 0\) continues to force \(Q = 0\), completely failing to hold a previous state of \(1\). Thus, Option (C) is incorrect.
  • Option (D): This circuit consists of cross-coupled NAND gates (an active-LOW latch). The node \(Q\) is given by \(Q = \overline{X_1 \cdot W}\). Applying \((X_1, X_2) = (1, 0)\) gives \(W = \overline{0 \cdot Q} = 1\), which leads to \(Q = \overline{1 \cdot 1} = 0\). This produces a low output instead of the required high state. Thus, Option (D) is incorrect.
Consequently, none of the provided circuit options produce the precise functional behavior required at the labeled terminal \(Q\), rendering all options incorrect. \[\boxed{\text{None of the options are correct.}}\]
Key points
  • Derive the functional truth table behavior directly from the waveform transitions: \((X_1, X_2) = (1,0) \rightarrow \text{Set } (Q=1)\), and \((0,1) \rightarrow \text{Reset } (Q=0)\).
  • To verify a circuit configuration, evaluate the boolean logic equation specifically at the node labeled \(Q\) to ensure it satisfies the functional criteria.
  • The orientation or placement of terminal nodes can vary arbitrarily; the input steering connections relative to the labeled terminal dictate the final stable state.

questions.question: A digital-to-analog converter with a full-scale output voltage of 3.5,V has a resolution close to 14,mV. Its bit size is
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Full-scale output voltage of DAC: \(V_{FS} = 3.5\,\text{V}\)
  • Resolution: \(R \approx 14\,\text{mV} = 14 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{V}\)
Resolution of a DAC is given by: \[R = \frac{V_{fullscale}}{2^n - 1}\] Substituting the given values: \[2^n - 1 = \frac{3.5}{14 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{3.5}{0.014} = 250\] \[2^n = 251\] Taking the natural logarithm on both sides: \[n \ln(2) = \ln(251)\] \[n = \frac{\ln(251)}{\ln(2)} = \frac{5.5255}{0.6931} \approx 7.97 \approx 8\] Since \(n\) must always be an integer: Its bit size is \(\mathbf{8}\).
Key points
  • DAC Resolution: \(R = \dfrac{V_{FS}}{2^n - 1}\), where \(n\) is the number of bits and \(V_{FS}\) is the full-scale output voltage.
  • Resolution can also be expressed as a percentage: \(R(\%) = \dfrac{1}{2^n - 1} \times 100\%\).
  • For an \(n\)-bit DAC, there are \(2^n\) possible output levels and \(2^n - 1\) steps.

questions.question: If \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are the inputs to the circuit shown in the figure, the output \(Q\) is
questions.explanation:
Given logic circuit is shown below,
This is a digital logic circuit implemented using NMOS transistors with enhancement-load NMOS pull-up devices. Consider the left part of the circuit. When \(X_1=1\), transistor \(Q_1\) turns ON and pulls node \(Y_1\) to ground. Hence, \[Y_1 = 0\] When \(X_1=0\), transistor \(Q_1\) turns OFF and the load transistor pulls \(Y_1\) HIGH. Hence, \[Y_1 = 1\] Therefore, the left stage acts as an inverter: \[Y_1=\overline{X_1}\] Now consider the right part of the circuit. Transistors \(Q_2\) and \(Q_3\) are connected in parallel between the output node and ground. If either \(Y_1\) or \(X_2\) is HIGH, the corresponding NMOS transistor turns ON and pulls the output LOW. Thus, the right stage implements a NOR gate. Hence, \[Q=\overline{Y_1+X_2}\] Substituting \(Y_1=\overline{X_1}\), \[Q=\overline{\overline{X_1}+X_2}\] Using De Morgan's theorem, \[Q=X_1\cdot\overline{X_2}\] Therefore, (D) \(X_1\cdot\overline{X_2}\)
Key points
  • An NMOS transistor acts as a pull-down device. When its gate input is HIGH, it connects the output node to ground.
  • An enhancement-load NMOS inverter realizes the logic function \[Y=\overline{X}.\]
  • Parallel NMOS pull-down transistors implement a NOR function because any HIGH input can pull the output LOW.
  • The overall circuit consists of an inverter followed by a NOR gate.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not analyze the right stage directly using \(X_1\) and \(X_2\); first determine the intermediate node \(Y_1\).
  • Remember that parallel NMOS pull-down paths realize a NOR gate, whereas series NMOS pull-down paths realize a NAND gate.
  • Apply De Morgan's theorem carefully: \[\overline{A+B}=\overline{A}\,\overline{B}.\]

Method 1
Block Diagram Reduction : img/ch3_time_response_analysis/3_05_1.jpg \[E(s) = R(s) - Y(s)\] The output response \(Y(s)\) is given by: \[Y(s) = \left[ \{R(s) - Y(s)\}\frac{3}{s} - R(s) \right] \frac{2}{s+2}\] \[Y(s)\left[ 1 + \frac{6}{s(s+2)} \right] = R(s)\left[ \frac{6 - 2s}{s(s+2)} \right]\] \[Y(s) = R(s)\frac{6 - 2s}{s^2 + 2s + 6}\] \[E(s) = R(s) - \frac{6 - 2s}{s^2 + 2s + 6}R(s)\] \[E(s) = R(s)\left[ \frac{s^2 + 4s}{s^2 + 2s + 6} \right]\] For a unit step input \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\), the steady-state error \(e_{ss}\) via Final Value Theorem is: \[e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} sE(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{1}{s} \frac{s^2 + 4s}{s^2 + 2s + 6} \right] = 0\]
Method 2

\[\dfrac{Y(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{P_1\Delta_1 + P_2\Delta_2}{\Delta} = \frac{6 - 2s}{s^2 + 2s + 6}\] The error expression is \(E(s) = R(s)[1 - \dfrac{Y(s)}{R(s)}]\) \[E(s)= R(s)\left[\frac{s^2 + 4s}{s^2 + 2s + 6}\right]\] For \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\): \(e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \dfrac{1}{s} \left[\dfrac{s^2 + 4s}{s^2 + 2s + 6}\right] = 0\)
\[\boxed{(C) \ \ 0}\]

questions.question: A unity feedback system, having an open loop gain \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K(1-s)}{(1+s)}\), becomes stable when
questions.explanation:
Given open-loop transfer function: \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K(1-s)}{(1+s)}\) The characteristic equation (C.E.) of the unity feedback system is defined as: \[1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\] \[1 + \frac{K(1-s)}{1+s} = 0 \implies s(1-K) + (K+1) = 0\] Solving for the closed-loop pole \(s\): \[s = -\frac{(K+1)}{1-K} = \frac{K+1}{K-1}\] The system becomes stable only when the root lies in the left-half of the \(s\)-plane (i.e., \(s\) must be negative). Case 1:
\[(K+1) > 0 \quad \text{\&} \quad (K-1) < 0\] \[K > -1 \quad \text{\&} \quad K < 1\] \[\implies |K| < 1\] Case 2:
\[(K+1) < 0 \quad \text{\&} \quad (K-1) > 0\] \[K < -1 \quad \text{\&} \quad K > 1\] \[\implies \text{Not possible}\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ |K| < 1}\]

  • The number of asymptotes is given by \(P - Z\) = 3
  • Since all branches terminate at infinity, the system does not have any finite zeros (\(Z = 0\)). Thus, the number of open-loop poles is: \(P = 3\)
  • The centroid (intersection of asymptotes on the real axis) is located at the origin (\(\sigma = 0\)).
  • Since all three branches originate from the origin, all three open-loop poles must be located precisely at the origin (\(s = 0, 0, 0\)).
Therefore, the open-loop transfer function (O.L.T.F.) is: \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{s^3}\) \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{K}{s^3}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Misinterpreting Centroid Intersection: Avoid assuming that if asymptotes pass through the origin, it always means all individual poles are at zero; it simply means the average position (\(\sum \text{poles}\)) is zero. However, since the branches originate directly out of the origin in all three directions, the individual pole locations themselves must be at \(s = 0\).

questions.explanation: When we see the equivalent circuit of a transformer referred to the primary side, the primary leakage reactance and secondary leakage reactance are comparable in value. But the magnetizing reactance has a very large value in comparison to leakage reactance because magnetizing reactance represents flux linkage in the core. \[\text{Primary leakage reactance}=\text{secondary leakage reactance}\] \[X_{1}=X_{2}^{\prime}\] Also, the magnetizing reactance is much larger than leakage reactance, \[X_{m}\gg X_{1},\;X_{2}^{\prime}\] Hence, \[X_{1}=X_{2}^{\prime}\ll X_{m}\] \[\boxed{D}\]

Statement for Linked Questions Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2:
A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

Two magnetic poles revolve around a stationary armature carrying two coils \((c_1-c_1',\, c_2-c_2')\) as shown in Fig.,3.05.1. Consider the instant when the poles are in a position as shown. Identify the correct statement regarding the polarity of the induced emf at this instant in coil sides \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: Assume the poles are stationary and the rotor rotates in the anti-clockwise direction. This causes the same relative motion between conductors and magnetic field. The induced emf in a conductor is given by \[e = |\vec{V} \times \vec{B}|\] The magnetic field is directed from North pole to South pole, i.e., from right to left. For conductors belonging to coil \(C_2\), the velocity of conductors is parallel or anti-parallel to the magnetic field. Hence, \[\vec{V} \times \vec{B} = 0\] and no emf is induced in coil \(C_2\). For conductors belonging to coil \(C_1\), the conductor velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field. Therefore, \[|\vec{V} \times \vec{B}|\] is maximum and the induced emf in coil \(C_1\) is maximum. Using Fleming's right-hand rule, the direction of induced emf is outward for conductor \(C_1\) and inward for the opposite conductor of the same coil. Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{A}\]

A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

A \(50\,\text{kW}\) dc shunt motor is loaded to draw the rated armature current at any given speed. When driven (i) at half the rated speed by armature voltage control and (ii) at \(1.5\) times the rated speed by field control, the respective output powers delivered by the motor are approximately
questions.explanation:
In armature voltage control, the DC motor operates as a constant torque drive. \[P=T\omega\] Since torque remains constant, \[P\propto \omega\] At half the rated speed, \[P_2=\frac{1}{2}P_1 =\frac{1}{2}\times 50 =25\,\text{kW}\] In field control, the motor operates as a constant power drive. Therefore, \[P=50\,\text{kW}\] \[\boxed{B}\] [figure unavailable]
Key points
  • Armature voltage control is used below rated speed and provides constant torque operation.
  • For constant torque drives, \(P=T\omega \Rightarrow P\propto\omega\).
  • Field control is used above rated speed and provides constant power operation.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse field control with constant torque operation.
  • At half speed under constant torque operation, power becomes half.

In relation to DC machines, match the following and choose the correct combination.

Statement for Linked Questions (Q4.07.3,Q4.07.4 and Q4.07.5):
A three phase squirrel cage induction motor has a starting current of seven times the full load current and full load slip of \(5\%\).

On the torque/speed curve of induction motor shown in Fig.4.05.1, four points of operation are marked as W, X, Y, and Z. Which one of them represents the operation at a slip greater than \(1\)? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Slip greater than unity indicates that the induction machine is operating in the braking (plugging) region. In the motoring region, \[s=\frac{N_{s}-N_{r}}{N_{s}}<1\] In the braking (plugging) region, the rotor rotates opposite to the rotating magnetic field. Therefore, \[s=\frac{N_{s}+N_{r}}{N_{s}}>1\] Since the rotor and rotating magnetic field move in opposite directions, the developed torque opposes the rotor motion, producing braking action. Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Motoring operation: \(0<s<1\).
  • Generating operation: \(s<0\).
  • Plugging (braking) operation: \(s>1\).
  • During plugging, torque and rotor speed act in opposite directions.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Assuming slip cannot exceed unity.
  • Confusing plugging operation with generating operation.
  • Using \(s=\dfrac{N_{s}-N_{r}}{N_{s}}\) in the braking region where rotor rotates opposite to the field.
  • Forgetting that braking torque opposes the direction of rotor motion.

Under no load condition, if the applied voltage to an induction motor is reduced from the rated voltage to half the rated value,
options: the speed decreases and the stator current increases
both the speed and the stator current decrease
the speed and the stator current remain practically constant
there is negligible change in the speed but the stator current decreases
questions.explanation: At no-load, the slip of an induction motor is nearly zero. Therefore, the rotor branch of the equivalent circuit can be neglected and the circuit reduces to the shunt magnetizing branch. \[Z=\left(R_{c}\right)\parallel \left(jX_{m}\right)\] The no-load current is \[I_{0}=\frac{V}{|Z|}\] If the supply voltage \(V\) is reduced, the no-load current \(I_{0}\) also reduces approximately in the same proportion. However, since the motor is operating at no-load, \[s \approx 0\] and hence the rotor speed is nearly equal to synchronous speed, \[N_{r}\approx N_{s}\] \[N_{s}=\frac{120f}{P}\] Since frequency remains unchanged, synchronous speed remains unchanged. Therefore, the no-load speed of the induction motor remains practically constant even though the supply voltage is reduced. \[N_{r}\approx N_{s}=\text{constant}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{D}\]

Determine the correctness or otherwise of the following Assertion [a] and the Reason [r]. Assertion: Under \(V/f\) control of induction motor, the maximum value of the developed torque remains constant over a wide range of speed in the sub-synchronous region. Reason: The magnetic flux is maintained almost constant at the rated value by keeping the ratio \(V/f\) constant over the considered speed range.
options: Both [a] and [r] are true and [r] is the correct reason for [a]
Both [a] and [r] are true but [r] is not the correct reason for [a]
questions.explanation: The resultant air-gap flux per pole is proportional to the ratio of voltage to frequency. \[\phi_{m}\propto \frac{V}{f}\] To avoid saturation of the stator and rotor cores, the flux must be kept constant. Therefore, \[\frac{V}{f}=\text{constant}\] The maximum torque of an induction motor is \[T_{\max}=\frac{3}{2\omega_{s}}\frac{V^{2}}{X_{2}^{\prime}}\] Since \[\omega_{s}\propto f\] and \[X_{2}^{\prime}\propto f\] therefore, \[T_{\max}\propto \frac{V^{2}}{f^{2}}\] or \[T_{\max}\propto \left(\frac{V}{f}\right)^{2}\] If both \(V\) and \(f\) are reduced while maintaining a constant \(\dfrac{V}{f}\) ratio, then \[T_{\max}=\text{constant}\] Hence, both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion. \[\boxed{A}\]

The input voltage given to a converter is \[v_i = 100\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\,\text{V}\] The current drawn by the converter is \[\begin{gathered} i_i=10\sqrt{2}\sin\left(100\pi t-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\ +5\sqrt{2}\sin\left(300\pi t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ +2\sqrt{2}\sin\left(500\pi t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\,\text{A} \end{gathered}\]

Consider a phase-controlled converter shown in the figure. The thyristor is fired at an angle \(\alpha\) in every positive half cycle of the input voltage. If the peak value of the instantaneous output voltage equals \(230\,\text{V}\), the firing angle \(\alpha\) is close to [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Given, \[V_{\text{rms}}=230\,\text{V}\] Therefore, \[V_m=230\sqrt{2}\,\text{V}\] For \(\alpha>90^\circ\), the peak output voltage is \[V_{o,\text{peak}}=V_m\sin\alpha\] Given, \[V_{o,\text{peak}}=230\,\text{V}\] \[230=230\sqrt{2}\sin\alpha\] \[\sin\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\] Since firing angle is in the second quadrant, \[\alpha=135^\circ\] \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]
Key points
  • For a half-wave controlled rectifier, if \(\alpha<90^\circ\), the peak output is \(V_m\).
  • If \(\alpha>90^\circ\), the peak output occurs at firing instant and equals \(V_m\sin\alpha\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not take \(230\,\text{V}\) as the peak value of the input voltage; it is RMS.
  • Do not choose \(\alpha=45^\circ\) because firing angle must be greater than \(90^\circ\) for reduced peak output.

questions.question: A \(1000\,\text{V}\) DC supply has two single-core cables as its positive and negative leads; their insulation resistances to earth are \(4\,\text{M}\Omega\) and \(6\,\text{M}\Omega\), respectively, as shown in the given figure. A voltmeter with resistance \(50\,\text{k}\Omega\) is used to measure the insulation of the cable. When connected between the positive core and earth, then voltmeter reads [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Given:
\[V_s=1000\,\text{V},\qquad R_1=4\,\text{M}\Omega,\qquad R_2=6\,\text{M}\Omega,\qquad R_v=50\,\text{k}\Omega=0.05\,\text{M}\Omega\] The voltmeter is connected between the positive core and earth, so it is in parallel with \(R_1\). Step 1: Equivalent resistance of \(R_1\) and voltmeter
\[R_{eq}=R_1\parallel R_v=\frac{4\times0.05}{4+0.05}=0.0494\,\text{M}\Omega\] Thus the circuit becomes \(R_{eq}\) in series with \(R_2\). Step 2: Total resistance
\[R_T=R_{eq}+R_2=0.0494+6=6.0494\,\text{M}\Omega\] Step 3: Circuit current
\[I=\frac{V_s}{R_T}=\frac{1000}{6.0494\times10^6}=165.3\,\mu\text{A}\] Step 4: Voltmeter reading (across \(R_{eq}\))
\[V_v=IR_{eq}=165.3\times10^{-6}\times0.0494\times10^6=8.16\,\text{V}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }8\,\text{V}}\]

questions.explanation: A Q-meter is used to measure: \[\text{Quality factor }(Q)\] of coils and resonant circuits. It operates on the principle of series resonance. At resonance: \[X_L=X_C\] Hence the circuit impedance becomes minimum and current becomes maximum. The quality factor is given by: \[Q=\frac{V_C}{V}\] where: \[V_C=\text{voltage across capacitor},\qquad V=\text{applied voltage}\] Thus the Q-meter measures voltage magnification in a series resonant circuit. Therefore, the correct option is: \[\boxed{\textbf{C. Series resonance}}\]
